“Simple” Systems – Linear Algebra Version

Let the standard basis vectors be \(\vec{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vec{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\).

NameSystem (Matrix Form)General Solution
Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C\,\vec{e}_1\,e^{at} + D\,\vec{e}_2\,e^{bt}\)
Partially Coupled \(\vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix} a & 1 \\ 0 & a \end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = \bigl(C\,\vec{e}_1 + D(\vec{e}_1\,t + \vec{e}_2)\bigr)e^{at}\)

Page 6

Systems of First-Order Equations with Constant Coefficients

Homogeneous Case

Suppose \(a, b, c, d\) are real constants. Consider the system:

\[ \frac{dx}{dt} = ax + by, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = cx + dy \]

Setting \(\vec{r} = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}\), we can rewrite this system as:

\[ \vec{r}\,' = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \vec{r} \]

Any homogeneous linear system with constant coefficients can be written compactly as \(\vec{r}\,' = A\vec{r}\) for a constant matrix \(A\).

Page 7

Collinearity & Determinant

Definition (Collinear Vectors): Two vectors are collinear if they lie on the same line through the origin. That is, \(\vec{u}\) and \(\vec{v}\) are collinear if one is a scalar multiple of the other.

Handwritten diagram showing two vectors \(\vec{u}\) and \(\vec{v}\) pointing along the same line through the origin, illustrating the concept of collinearity.

Page 8

Collinearity & Determinant

For a matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\), the columns are collinear if and only if they have the same slope.

Comparing slopes leads to the condition \(ad - bc = 0\), which motivates the following definition.

Definition (Determinant): For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\), the determinant of \(A\) is

\[ \det(A) = ad - bc. \]

Fact: The columns of \(A\) are collinear (i.e., linearly dependent) if and only if \(\det(A) = 0\).

Page 9

Collinearity & Determinant – Practice

Compute by hand the determinant of the following matrix:

\[ \det\!\left(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ -4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\right) = \;? \]

Using the formula \(\det(A) = ad - bc\):

\[ \det\!\left(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ -4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\right) = (-1)(5) - (2)(-4) = -5 + 8 = 3. \]

Page 10

Basis & Coordinates

Definition (Basis): Two nonzero, non-collinear vectors in the plane form a basis (they are linearly independent).

Fact: Fix a basis \(\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2\}\) of the plane. Every vector in the plane can be written as a unique linear combination of the basis vectors.

Page 11

New Conceptualization: Changing Labels

A key idea is that choosing a different basis is equivalent to relabeling points in the plane. The physical location of a vector \(\vec{w}\) does not change; only the coordinates (labels) we assign to it change depending on the basis we use.

The slide shows an arrow labeled \(\vec{w}\) drawn in the standard coordinate plane, with the word “Destination” indicating the tip of the vector. This sets up the visual idea that the same point can be reached (described) using different coordinate systems.

Page 12

New Conceptualization: Changing Labels (continued)

In the standard basis, the vector \(\vec{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\) is plotted on the standard coordinate grid.

A standard Cartesian grid is shown with axes labeled from approximately −2 to 6 horizontally and 0 to 5 vertically. The vector \(\vec{w}\) is drawn with its tip at the point \((1, 5)\) in standard coordinates.

Page 13

New Conceptualization: Changing Labels (continued)

For comparison, the vector \(\vec{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\) is shown alongside the standard basis vectors \(\vec{e}_1\) and \(\vec{e}_2\).

The same coordinate grid now includes the standard basis vectors \(\vec{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vec{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\) drawn at the origin, alongside the vector \(\vec{w}\). This highlights that \(\vec{w} = 1\cdot\vec{e}_1 + 5\cdot\vec{e}_2\) in the standard basis.

Page 14

New Conceptualization: Changing Labels (continued)

Now introduce a new basis \(\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2\}\). The same vector \(\vec{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\) can also be written as:

\[ \vec{w} = 3\,\vec{v}_1 + 2\,\vec{v}_2 \]

so its label in the new basis is \([\vec{w}]_B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

The coordinate grid now shows basis vectors \(\vec{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vec{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) drawn at the origin. The vector \(\vec{w}\) is shown reaching its tip, and the coordinates \(\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}\) are labeled as its representation in the \(B\)-basis.

Page 15

Coordinate Vector

Definition (B-Coordinate Vector): Fix an ordered basis \(B = \{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2\}\). For each \(\vec{w} \in \mathbb{R}^2\), the unique coefficients \((x_1, x_2)\) such that \(\vec{w} = x_1\vec{v}_1 + x_2\vec{v}_2\) define the \(B\)-coordinate vector of \(\vec{w}\), denoted

\[ [\vec{w}]_B = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The coordinate vector is the label we assign to a point in the basis \(B\).

Page 16

Example: Coordinate Vector

Let \(B = \left\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2\right\} = \left\{\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\right\}\).

Observe that \(\vec{w} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\5\end{bmatrix}\) and \([\vec{w}]_B = \begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}\).

This means \(\vec{w} = 3\,\vec{v}_1 + 2\,\vec{v}_2 = 3\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} + 2\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\3\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}-2\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\5\end{bmatrix}\). ✓

A coordinate grid is shown with the \(B\)-basis grid overlaid. The vectors \(\vec{v}_1\) and \(\vec{v}_2\) are drawn at the origin forming a new grid. The point \(\vec{w}\) is labeled both with its standard coordinates \(\begin{bmatrix}1\\5\end{bmatrix}\) and its \(B\)-coordinates \(\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}\).

Page 17

Matrix Multiplication as Label Change

Given the ordered basis \(B = \{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2\}\), define the change-of-basis matrix

\[ P_B = [\vec{v}_1 \mid \vec{v}_2] \]

as the matrix whose columns are the basis vectors. Then:

\[ \vec{w} = x_1\vec{v}_1 + x_2\vec{v}_2 = P_B \begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix} = P_B\,[\vec{w}]_B \]

Key fact: Multiplication by \(P_B\) converts a \(B\)-label to the standard label.

Page 18

Example: Matrix Multiplication as Label Change

With \(B = \left\{\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\right\}\), we have \(P_B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\).

\[ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{P_B} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}}_{[\vec{w}]_B} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1\\5\end{bmatrix}}_{\vec{w}} \]

Verification: \(3\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} + 2\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\3\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}-2\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\5\end{bmatrix}\). ✓

The same \(B\)-coordinate grid from the previous example is shown again for reference, with \(\vec{v}_1\), \(\vec{v}_2\), the point \(\vec{w}\), and its \(B\)-label all labeled.

Page 19

2×2 Inverse

Definition (Matrix Inverse): The inverse of a 2×2 matrix \(A\) reverses the process of multiplying by \(A\). That is, \(A^{-1}\) is the matrix such that for all \(\vec{r}\),

\[ A^{-1}(A\vec{r}) = \vec{r}. \]

Fact: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}a & b\\c & d\end{bmatrix}\) with \(\det(A) = ad - bc \neq 0\),

\[ A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b\\-c & a\end{bmatrix}. \]

Page 20

Example: Computing the Inverse

Continuing the example with \(P_B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\), we compute \(P_B^{-1}\).

Since \(\det(P_B) = (1)(1) - (-1)(1) = 1 + 1 = 2\),

\[ P_B^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\\-1 & 1\end{bmatrix}. \]

Verification that \(P_B^{-1}\vec{w} = [\vec{w}]_B\):

\[ \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\\-1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\5\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1+5\\-1+5\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}6\\4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}. \checkmark \]

Key fact: Multiplication by \(P_B^{-1}\) converts a standard label to the \(B\)-label.

Page 21

Similar Matrix Decompositions (SMDs) and First-Order Systems

Definition (Similar Matrix Decomposition): A similar matrix decomposition (SMD) for a matrix \(A\) is a factorization

\[ A = P B P^{-1} \]

where \(P = P_B = [\vec{v}_1 \mid \vec{v}_2]\) is a coordinate-change matrix and \(B\) is a geometrically simpler transformation.

Page 22

SMDs and First-Order Systems (continued)

For a matrix \(A = PBP^{-1}\), multiplication by \(A\) can be understood in three steps:

  1. Step 1: Apply \(P^{-1}\) – convert from standard label to \(B\)-label.
  2. Step 2: Apply \(B\) – perform the geometry in the \(B\)-label coordinate system.
  3. Step 3: Apply \(P\) – convert from \(B\)-label back to standard label.

Page 23

SMDs and First-Order Systems (continued)

Suppose \(\vec{r}\,' = A\vec{r}\) and \(A = PBP^{-1}\). Then:

\[ \vec{r}\,' = PBP^{-1}\vec{r} \]

Let \(\vec{s} = P^{-1}\vec{r}\) (i.e., \(\vec{r} = P\vec{s}\)). Substituting:

\[ P\vec{s}\,' = PBP^{-1}(P\vec{s}) = PB\vec{s} \] \[ \vec{s}\,' = B\vec{s} \]

In the \(B\)-coordinates, the system \(\vec{s}\,' = B\vec{s}\) has the simple form (uncoupled, partially coupled, or complex uncoupled), which we already know how to solve.

Page 24

Systems – Linear Algebra Version (General Basis)

Let \(\vec{v}_1\) and \(\vec{v}_2\) be basis vectors with change-of-basis matrix \(P = [\vec{v}_1 \mid \vec{v}_2]\).

NameSystemGeneral Solution
Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = P\begin{bmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C\,\vec{v}_1\,e^{at} + D\,\vec{v}_2\,e^{bt}\)
Partially Coupled \(\vec{r}\,' = P\begin{bmatrix}a&1\\0&a\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = \bigl(C\,\vec{v}_1 + D(\vec{v}_1\,t + \vec{v}_2)\bigr)e^{at}\)
Complex Uncoupled \(\vec{r}\,' = P\begin{bmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{bmatrix}P^{-1}\vec{r}\) \(\vec{r}(t) = C_1\bigl(\cos(bt)\,\vec{v}_1 + \sin(bt)\,\vec{v}_2\bigr)e^{at} + C_2\bigl(-\sin(bt)\,\vec{v}_1 + \cos(bt)\,\vec{v}_2\bigr)e^{at}\)

Note: All \(\vec{e}_i\)’s from the standard-basis version become \(\vec{v}_i\)’s.
